About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Visual Arts – Painting Years 12–13
of the New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Visual Arts – Painting Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Visual Arts – Painting Years 12–13 is proposed
to be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Visual Arts – Painting Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year
12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.




Visual Arts – Painting | Years 12–13 | October 2026                                       Page 2

Purpose statement
                                                                   Te toi whakairo, ka ihiihi, ka wehiwehi, ka aweawe       Artistic excellence makes the world sit up in wonder.
                                                                   te ao katoa.




  In Visual Arts – Painting, students are taught how ideas, meaning, and visual                  Visual Arts – Painting leads to pathways in creative and cultural industries,
  language are developed and communicated. Students learn to investigate,                        including fine arts, illustration, concept art, visual communication, creative
  generate, and refine artistic ideas in response to a central proposition, drawing on           technologies, and gallery and museum practice.
  established practice, personal experience, and a range of cultural, social,
  historical, and art historical contexts.

Students are taught how painting conventions, materials, techniques, and processes
express meaning in artworks. They develop knowledge of visual elements such as
colour, composition, gesture, surface, mark-making, and the material properties of
paint, and learn how these can be manipulated to communicate ideas with increasing
clarity, depth, and intention.

Painting provides students with conceptual and procedural knowledge to investigate,
analyse, evaluate, and apply understanding through sustained artmaking. Through
engagement with established practice and their own creative development, students
learn to respond critically to contexts and perspectives, examine how meaning is
constructed in artworks, and make purposeful artistic decisions informed by
investigation, experimentation, and reflection.

As students progress through Years 12 and 13, they develop increasingly sustained
studio practice, artistic agency, and critical judgement. They generate, refine, and
present a coherent body of work that demonstrates critical thinking, technical control,
material awareness, and a personal painterly voice.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.

 In Visual Arts – Painting, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to analyse established practice and communicate the creative ideas, processes, intentions, and meanings in own and others’
 artwork.

The teaching of all knowledge and practices is compulsory. However, schools can
determine how learning is organised across the year, including integrating content
from multiple elements and strands where this supports coherence and depth.
Examples within the teaching sequence in brackets and labelled ‘e.g.’ are provided as
guidance only; as long as the intended knowledge and practices are met, schools and
teachers may substitute contexts and examples that better reflect local environments,
iwi and hapū connections, cultural knowledge, communities and contexts, student
interests, and teacher expertise.

Disciplinary writing is included in the teaching sequence to set out what subject-
specific literacy is to be taught. It is organised into a knowledge component that is
consistent across all year levels and a practice component sequenced across years.

 Responsible use of artificial intelligence

 Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues relating to
 ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking, source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-making. Responsible AI use
 emphasises the importance of exercising independent judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent about AI use, considering diverse
 perspectives, and developing independent thinking.
